Or it is an object of purpose (maf'ūl lahu), meaning: He subjected it upon them for the purpose of uprooting.

'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Zurarah al-Kilabi said:

*So time separated between them, a time in which consecutive years were ḥusūm (ruinous).*

[Of 'Abd al-'Aziz ibn Zurarah al-Kilabi. The original statement is: "fa-farraqa baynahum zamān" — "so time separated them." We carried you (ﷺ) — we carried your forefathers in the sailing ship (al-jariyah), since if they were descendants of those carried and saved, the carrying of their forefathers was a favour upon them, as though they themselves were the ones carried, because their salvation was the cause of their being born.

﴿That We might make it﴾: the pronoun refers to the act, namely the salvation of the believers and the drowning of the disbelievers.

﴿a reminder﴾: an admonition and a lesson.

﴿and that a retaining ear may retain it﴾: an ear that is apt to be attentive and to preserve what it has heard, and not to waste it by abandoning action. It was also read as "wa-taʿiyaha" with the ʿayn vowelless, for lightness: [the verb] wa'a is likened to kabd (liver).

The verb is attributed to the verbal noun, and its feminine marker is omitted because of the separation. Al-Zamakhshari (Mahmud) says: "If you say, why does he say *wahidah* when they are two blasts...?" Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) says: "As for the benefit of indicating the greatness of this blast: the one that causes the earth and mountains to be leveled and the world to be ruined is by itself, needing no second."

I say its meaning is that it is not repeated at its time. If you ask, "Which of the two blasts is it?", I say it is the first, because with it the world is corrupted. This is also the report from Ibn Abbas, though it is also reported from him that it is the second.

I say: He made "the day" a name for the extended time in which the two blasts, the swoon, the resurrection, the standing and the reckoning take place. Therefore it is said *yawma'idhin tu'radun*, just as you say: "I came to him in such-and-such a year," while your coming was at one of its times.

It is also read *wa-hummilat* (with the carrier omitted), which is one of three possibilities.

"And they are leveled" means the two masses, the mass of the lands and the mass of the mountains, are struck against one another until they are crushed and return as a heap of sand, scattered dust. *Dakk* is more intensive than *daqq*. It is also said that they are spread out in one spreading, becoming a flat land in which you see no crookedness or hillock, from your saying *indakka al-sanam* when the hump flattens; a camel is *adakk*, a she-camel *dakkaa'*, and from this comes *al-dukkan* (the raised bench).

He means: the creation that is called the angels, and the pronoun referring to it in His saying *fawqahum* (above them) is returned in the plural in accordance with the meaning.

If you ask, "What is the difference between His saying *wal-malaku* (and the angel) and saying *wal-malaaika* (and the angels)?" I say: *malak* is more general than *malaaika*. Do you not see that your saying "There is no angel but he is a witness" is more general than your saying "There are no angels but they are witnesses."

The singular is *ruja*, shortened; that is, it splits, and it is the dwelling of the angels, so they withdraw (*fa-yandawuna*) to its extremities and what surrounds it from its borders. [Ahmad: Both are defined as the generic definite, so singular and plural are equal in generality.]

"Eight": that is, eight of them. And from the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "They are four today; when the Day of Resurrection comes, God will strengthen them with four others, and they will be eight." Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 69, verse 19–24:

فَأَمَّا تفصيل للعرض. ها: صوت يصوت به فيفهم منه معنى «خذ» كأف وحس، وما أشبه ذلك [[قوله «كأف وحس، وما أشبه ذلك» يفهم من كل منهما معنى التضجر والتألم، كما يفيده الصحاح. (ع)]].

[Translation of the above: "Fa-amma" is a detailed explanation of the presentation. "Ha": a sound uttered by which the meaning of "take" is understood, like "uff" and "hass", and the like. [Note: the words "like uff and hass, and the like" convey, from each of them, the meaning of displeasure and pain, as the Sihah (of al-Jawhari) indicates. (Ed.)]]

وكِتابِيَهْ منصوب بهاؤم عند الكوفيين، وعند البصريين باقرءوا، لأنه أقرب العاملين. وأصله: هاؤم كتابي اقرؤا كتابي، فحذف الأوّل لدلالة الثاني عليه.

"Ha" for pausing (haa al-sakt) in "kitabiyah," and likewise in "hisabiyah," "maliyah," and "sultaniyah." The right of these "ha"s is that they be pronounced in pause and dropped in continuation, [Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said: "The right of these ha's, meaning in kitabiyah, hisabiyah, maliyah, and sultaniyah ... etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: Justifying the recitation by following the Mushaf is strange, given that the true belief is that the seven readings, in all their details, are transmitted by mass transmission (tawatur) from the Prophet (ﷺ), so whoever affirmed the "ha" in continuation affirmed it from the mass-transmitted recitation of the Prophet (ﷺ) as it was recited before it was written in the Mushaf. These people only introduce ijtihad into the widely transmitted readings, and believe that among them there is what was taken by theoretical choice, and this is an error whose door should not be opened, for it is a means to something greater. I once had a discussion with Shaykh Abu 'Amr, may Allah have mercy on him, concerning His words "And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger and fears Allah and keeps his duty to Him" (24:52) according to the reading of Hafs, which ended with my obliging the rejection of those who affirm the "ha" in continuation in the words of Surat al-Haqqah, because I argued against him with the affirmation of the famous readers of it so; I understood from his rejection of that what the words of al-Zamakhshari here conveyed, but I did not accept it from him, may Allah have mercy on him, so he retracted from it. This discussion was by correspondence between me and him, and it was the last of what was written of the sciences, as his close associates informed me, and that is correct, for it was at the beginning of his illness, may Allah have mercy on him. وقيل: لا بأس بالوصل والإسقاط. وقرأ ابن محيصن بإسكان الياء بغير هاء. وقرأ جماعة بإثبات الهاء في الوصل والوقف جميعا لاتباع المصحف ظَنَنْتُ علمت. وإنما أجرى الظن مجرى العلم، لأن الظن الغالب يقام مقام العلم في العادات والأحكام. ويقال: أظن ظنا كاليقين أنّ الأمر كيت وكيت راضِيَةٍ منسوبة إلى الرضا، كالدارع والنابل. والنسبة نسبتان:

It is said: there is no harm in both continuing and omitting. Ibn Muhaysin read with the yaa sakin without a "ha." A group read with affirming the "ha" both in continuation and in pause, to follow the Mushaf. "Zanantu" means "I knew." He treated "zann" (supposition) as "ilm" (knowledge), because strong supposition is placed in the position of knowledge in customary matters and in rulings. It is said: "azunnu zannan ka-l-yaqin" (I suppose a supposition like certainty) that the matter is such and such. "Radiyah" (pleasing) is attributed to "ridha" (pleasure), like "dari'" (armoured) and "nabil" (archer). Attribution is of two kinds:

نسبة بالحرف، ونسبة بالصيغة. أو جعل الفعل لها مجازا وهو لصاحبها عالِيَةٍ مرتفعة المكان في السماء. أو رفيعة الدرجات. أو رفيعة المبانى والقصور والأشجار دانِيَةٌ ينالها القاعد والنائم. يقال لهم كُلُوا وَاشْرَبُوا هَنِيئاً [[قوله «كلوا واشربوا هنيئا» في الصحاح: هنؤ الطعام وهنيء، أى: صار هنيئا. وهنأنى الطعام يهنئني ويهنؤنى، ولا نظير له في المهموز هنأ وهناء. وهنئت الطعام، أى: تهنأت به، وكلوه هنيئا مريئا. Attribution by the letter, and attribution by the form. Or the verb is ascribed to it metaphorically while it belongs to its owner: "'aliyah" (lofty), elevated in place in the sky; or elevated in degrees; or elevated in buildings, palaces and trees. "Daniyah" (near), which is reached by the one sitting and the one lying. It will be said to them: "Eat and drink with ease" (haniy'an), eating and drinking with ease. Or "hanitum hanian" as a verbal noun. "Bima aslaftum" means by what you sent forward of righteous deeds, "fi al-ayyam al-khaliyah," in the past days, the days of the world that have passed.

وعن مجاهد: أيام الصيام، أى: كلوا واشربوا بدل ما أمسكتم عن الأكل والشرب لوجه الله.

From Mujahid: "the days of fasting," meaning: eat and drink in return for what you abstained from eating and drinking for the sake of Allah.

وروى. يقول الله عز وجل: يا أوليائى طالما نظرت إليكم في الدنيا وقد قلصت شفاهكم عن الأشربة، وغارت أعينكم، وخمصت بطونكم، فكونوا اليوم في نعيمكم، وكلوا واشربوا هنيئا بما أسلفتم في الأيام الخالية.

It is related that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: "O My friends, how often I looked upon you in the world while your lips were drawn back from drinks, your eyes were sunken, and your bellies were hollow. So be today in your bliss, and eat and drink with ease for what you sent forward in the past days."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 69, verses 38–43:

It is an oath by all things, in their totality and comprehensiveness, since they do not fall outside two categories: that which is seen and that which is not seen. It was also said: the world and the Hereafter, bodies and spirits, humankind and jinn, creation and the Creator, and the apparent and hidden blessings. ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an is the word of a noble messenger﴾, meaning: he recites it and speaks it in the capacity of a messenger from Allah. ﴿And it is not the word of a poet﴾, nor of a soothsayer, as you claim. The word "qalla" (little) here carries the meaning of "none": that is, you do not believe and you do not remember at all. The meaning is: how disbelieving you are, and how heedless you are. ﴿It is a revelation (tanzil) from the Lord of the worlds﴾. "Tanzil" is a predicate (khabar) explaining that it is the word of a messenger to whom it was sent down. Abu al-Sammal read "tanzilan," meaning: it was sent down as a revelation. It was also said that "the noble messenger" refers to Jibril (peace be upon him), and the statement ﴿and it is not the word of a poet﴾ is evidence that it refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), since the meaning is to establish that he is a messenger, not a poet or a soothsayer.

al-Taqawwul (التقوّل): the *ifti'āl* form (a morphological pattern, *ifti'āl*, here carrying a sense of effort or affectation) of *al-qawl* ("saying"). [Mahmud said: "al-taqawwul is an *ifti'āl* form of *al-qawl*, because there is affectation in it… etc." Ahmad said: The pattern *uqā'ūla* from *al-qawl*, which is a defective root, is, as you see, an anomaly outside the regular morphological rules (*al-qiyās al-taṣrīfī*). It is possible that *al-aqāwīl* is a plural of a plural, like *al-a'ānīm*, which is the plural of *aqwāl* and *an'ām*. This is the apparent view, and God knows best.] It is as if there is affectation in it, in the manner of the *mufta'il* form. They called the fabricated sayings *aqāwīl* as a diminutive and a belittling, as in your saying *al-a'ājīb* and *al-aḍāḥīk*, as if it were the plural of *uf'ūla* from *al-qawl*. The meaning is:

If he had claimed against Us something We had not said, We would have seized him by force and killed him, as kings do to someone who lies against them, punishing him at once in anger and vengeance. He depicts *qatl al-ṣabr* (killing by binding and holding the victim) in its image to make it more terrifying, namely that he is taken by the hand and his neck is struck.

He specified the right hand rather than the left because the executioner, when he wants to strike the back of the neck, takes hold with his left hand, and when he wants to strike the neck from the front and confront him with the sword, which is more painful for the one being executed since he sees the sword, he takes hold with his right hand.

The meaning of ﴿لَأَخَذْنا مِنْهُ بِالْيَمِينِ﴾ is: We would have seized his right hand, just as ﴿لَقَطَعْنا مِنْهُ الْوَتِينَ﴾ means: We would have cut his jugular. This is clear. *Al-watīn* is the *nayāṭ al-qalb* (the membrane or sinew attached to the heart), which is the *ḥabl al-warīd* (the jugular vein); if it is cut, its owner dies. It is recited *wa-law tuquwwila* in the passive voice. It is said that ﴿حاجِزِينَ﴾ is in the form that describes *aḥad* (anyone), because it has the sense of a group, and it is a word that occurs in general negation, where the singular, plural, masculine and feminine are equal. From it is His saying: ﴿لا نُفَرِّقُ بَيْنَ أَحَدٍ مِنْ رُسُلِهِ﴾ and ﴿لَسْتُنَّ كَأَحَدٍ مِنَ النِّساءِ﴾. The pronoun in *ʿanhu* refers to the killing, meaning: none of you can prevent him from that or repel it from him. Or it refers to the Messenger of God, meaning: you cannot restrain the killer from him or come between him and the Messenger. The address is to the people. Likewise in His saying: ﴿وَإِنَّا لَنَعْلَمُ أَنَّ مِنْكُمْ مُكَذِّبِينَ﴾, it is a threat against denial. It is also said that the address is to the Muslims. The meaning is that some of them will disbelieve in the Qur'an. ﴿وَإِنَّهُ لَحَسْرَةٌ عَلَى الْكافِرِينَ﴾: the pronoun refers to the Qur'an; it is a regret for the disbelievers who deny it, when they see the reward of those who believe in it. Or the pronoun refers to the denial, and that the Qur'an is ﴿لَحَقُّ الْيَقِينِ﴾ (certain truth), as in your saying: "He is the scholar, truly the scholar," and "the very scholar." The meaning is: the pure certainty, the unmixed certainty.

﴿فَسَبِّحْ بِاسْمِ رَبِّكَ الْعَظِيمِ﴾: glorify the Great Name by mentioning it, which is His saying "Subhān Allāh," and worship Him in gratitude for what He has favored you with through His revelation to you.

From the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Ḥāqqa, God will take his account with ease."

[Narrated by al-Tha'labī, al-Wāḥidī and Ibn Mardawayh, with a chain going back to Ubayy ibn Ka'b.]

From the Messenger of God (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Ḥāqqa, God will take his account with ease."

[Narrated by al-Tha'labī, al-Wāḥidī and Ibn Mardawayh, with a chain going back to Ubayy ibn Ka'b.]

al-Taqawwul (التقوّل): the *ifti'āl* form (a morphological pattern, *ifti'āl*, here carrying a sense of effort or affectation) of *al-qawl* ("saying"). [Mahmud said: "al-taqawwul is an *ifti'āl* form of *al-qawl*, because there is affectation in it… etc." Ahmad said: The pattern *uqā'ūla* from *al-qawl*, which is a defective root, is, as you see, an anomaly outside the regular morphological rules (*al-qiyās al-taṣrīfī*). It is possible that *al-aqāwīl* is a plural of a plural, like *al-a'ānīm*, which is the plural of *aqwāl* and *an'ām*. This is the apparent view, and God knows best.] It is as if there is affectation in it, in the manner of the *mufta'il* form. They called the fabricated sayings *aqāwīl* as a diminutive and a belittling, as in your saying *al-a'ājīb* and *al-aḍāḥīk*, as if it were the plural of *uf'ūla* from *al-qawl*. The meaning is:

If he had claimed against Us something We had not said, We would have seized him by force and killed him, as kings do to someone who lies against them, punishing him at once in anger and vengeance. He depicts *qatl al-ṣabr* (killing by binding and holding the victim) in its image to make it more terrifying, namely that he is taken by the hand and his neck is struck.

He specified the right hand rather than the left because the executioner, when he wants to strike the back of the neck, takes hold with his left hand, and when he wants to strike the neck from the front and confront him with the sword, which is more painful for the one being executed since he sees the sword, he takes hold with his right hand.

The meaning of ﴿لَأَخَذْنا مِنْهُ بِالْيَمِينِ﴾ is: We would have seized his right hand, just as ﴿لَقَطَعْنا مِنْهُ الْوَتِينَ﴾ means: We would have cut his jugular. This is clear. *Al-watīn* is the *nayāṭ al-qalb* (the membrane or sinew attached to the heart), which is the *ḥabl al-warīd* (the jugular vein); if it is cut, its owner dies. It is recited *wa-law tuquwwila* in the passive voice. It is said that ﴿حاجِزِينَ﴾ is in the form that describes *aḥad* (anyone), because it has the sense of a group, and it is a word that occurs in general negation, where the singular, plural, masculine and feminine are equal. From it is His saying: ﴿لا نُفَرِّقُ بَيْنَ أَحَدٍ مِنْ رُسُلِهِ﴾ and ﴿لَسْتُنَّ كَأَحَدٍ مِنَ النِّساءِ﴾. The pronoun in *ʿanhu* refers to the killing, meaning: none of you can prevent him from that or repel it from him. Or it refers to the Messenger of God, meaning: you cannot restrain the killer from him or come between him and the Messenger. The address is to the people. Likewise in His saying: ﴿وَإِنَّا لَنَعْلَمُ أَنَّ مِنْكُمْ مُكَذِّبِينَ﴾, it is a threat against denial. It is also said that the address is to the Muslims. The meaning is that some of them will disbelieve in the Qur'an. ﴿وَإِنَّهُ لَحَسْرَةٌ عَلَى الْكافِرِينَ﴾: the pronoun refers to the Qur'an; it is a regret for the disbelievers who deny it, when they see the reward of those who believe in it. Or the pronoun refers to the denial, and that the Qur'an is ﴿لَحَقُّ الْيَقِينِ﴾ (certain truth), as in your saying: "He is the scholar, truly the scholar," and "the very scholar." The meaning is: the pure certainty, the unmixed certainty.
